Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates text generation by leveraging the fact that large language models are often highly confident about the next few tokens. Instead of generating text one token at a time, which is slow because each step requires a full forward pass through the model, speculative decoding uses a smaller, faster "draft" model to predict a sequence of tokens. The main, larger model then evaluates this entire sequence in a single pass.

If the main model agrees with the draft model’s predictions, the entire sequence is accepted, and the process moves to the next chunk. This is a massive speedup because the expensive large model only performs one computation for multiple tokens. If the main model disagrees at any point, it rejects the draft from that point onward and generates the correct token itself, after which the process resumes.

The key insight is that this method does not change the output. The main model acts as the final arbiter. It only accepts tokens it would have generated anyway. If the draft model guesses wrong, the main model corrects it. Therefore, the final text is identical to what the main model would have produced if it had generated every token sequentially. The only difference is the speed at which it gets there.

This works because language models exhibit a "self-consistency" property: they are usually very confident about the next token, especially in predictable contexts. The draft model, being smaller and faster, can exploit this confidence to propose likely continuations. The main model’s role is simply to verify these proposals. By batching the verification of multiple tokens, speculative decoding reduces the number of expensive forward passes required, leading to significant latency improvements without sacrificing quality or altering the model’s intended output.

Each step requires a full forward pass through all the model's layers, and because the inputs are sequential, you can't parallelize the loop across steps. Speculative decoding attacks that serial bottleneck with a two-model trick. You pair your large, slow "determiner" model with a smaller, faster "proposer" model that has been trained to mimic the determiner's behavior. The proposer runs ahead and writes out a small draft—say, three or four tokens—without you waiting. You then hand that entire draft to the determiner in a single forward pass, asking it to evaluate every token in the sequence at once. Because that batched pass replaces what would have been several sequential passes, you get a throughput win even though the determiner is the expensive one.

If it says, "yes, I would have emitted that token with high confidence," you accept it and move on. If it disagrees—meaning the proposer hallucinated a token the determiner would not have chosen—you reject the draft from that point forward, re-run the draft from where things diverged, and retry. The determiner's acceptance check is a perfect simulation of what it would have generated on its own. You are not changing the model's weights, its temperature, its logits, or its training distribution. You are merely reordering and batching the same computations so they complete in fewer real-time steps.

In practice, the smaller model is cheap and fast enough that even a full reject-and-retry costs less than another sequential token. And because the proposer is a good mimic of the determiner, most of those drafted tokens get accepted. The net effect is that your end user sees text appear faster, but the characters on their screen are byte-for-byte identical to what the large model would have produced if you'd let it run alone, token by patient token.

plain.content:
When a hash map receives a key, it runs that key through a hash function, which produces a number that gets reduced—usually by taking its remainder against the table size—to index into a fixed array. The trouble is that this function isn't one-to-one: two entirely different keys can land on the same index. That's a collision, and the language of the map has to decide how to sort it out.

The two classic strategies differ in where they keep the second (and third, etc.) item. With chaining, each slot in the array points to a small linked list or tree of entries that share that index. To look up a key, you compute the index, then walk through the list until you find a matching key. This is conceptually simple and degrades gracefully—lookup cost grows only as the *number of collisions per slot* grows, not the table size—but it means extra pointer-chasing and a bit more memory overhead per node. With open addressing, the array itself holds the entries, and when the target slot is occupied, the probe function (linear, quadratic, or double hashing) steps to the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one or a matching key. The trade-off is that the array has to be significantly under full before performance degrades, because once a long run of occupied slots forms, every lookup and insertion in that region pays for it.

Either way, the real maintenance work is triggered by the load factor—the ratio of stored entries to slots. If that ratio climbs past a threshold (commonly around 0.7, though it depends on the implementation), the map resizes. It allocates a new backing array, typically twice the old size (or the next power of two, to keep the modulo operation cheap), and then walks through every entry in the old table, recomputing each key's index against the *new* size, and placing it into the fresh array. The old array is then discarded. The resize itself costs O(n) work, which looks bad on its face, but because the table only doubles and entries only move when the load factor crosses the threshold, those costly passes happen logarithmically rarely. Amortized over many operations, each insert, delete, or lookup still costs a constant number of steps on average—the occasional big reshuffle is paid for by the cheap operations that preceded it.

In practice, modern implementations often combine these ideas: they might use open addressing when the table is sparse and fall back to small per-slot chains if a few keys are pathologically stubborn, or they might use a technique called "cuckoo hashing" where a collision causes a displaced entry to be shoved into another slot in a controlled way. But the fundamental story is the same—some keys will always collide, and the map either shoves the extras into a side structure or probes forward for room, and whenever the table gets too crowded it quietly rebuilds itself larger so the probing and the chains stay short.

A hash map stores key-value pairs by first running the key through a hash function, which produces an integer that serves as an index into an array of slots called a table or buckets. The ideal scenario is that every key lands in its own distinct slot, so lookups take essentially one step. In practice, this is not guaranteed. Two different keys can produce the same hash value, a situation called a collision. When that happens, the hash map has to decide how to place the second (and any subsequent) keys so they don't overwrite each other.

There are two main strategies. In chaining, each slot in the table holds not just a single entry but a short list — often a linked list or a small dynamic array — of entries that all hash to that same slot. When a new key arrives and the slot already has something in it, the new entry is simply appended to that list. A lookup is then two-step: go to the slot, then walk the small list until the matching key is found. In open addressing, the table has no secondary structure at all; instead, the map probes outward. If a slot is occupied, it tries the next index (or a step computed from the original hash, in the case of quadratic or double hashing) and keeps going until it finds an empty slot to park the entry in. Lookups work the same way: try the slot, then follow the same probing sequence until the matching key is found or an empty slot confirms the key isn't present. Chaining tends to be simpler to implement and handle under heavy load, while open addressing is often faster for small tables and uses less memory overhead, but it degrades more noticeably as the table fills up.

The second question is when and why the table grows. As more keys are inserted, the table becomes more crowded. For chaining, this means the per-slot lists get longer and lookups slow down because you have to walk more elements. For open addressing, it means probes have to travel farther before finding a free slot, and in the worst case the probe sequence can wrap around the entire table before giving up. Both approaches stay fast only if collisions remain rare, which requires the table to have plenty of empty space relative to the number of entries. So every hash map tracks a ratio, the load factor, which is simply the number of entries divided by the total number of slots. When that ratio crosses a chosen threshold — commonly somewhere around 0.7 for open addressing or 0.75, and it varies by implementation — the map decides it is time to resize.

The resize works like this. The map allocates a new, larger table, most commonly twice the size of the old one, though some implementations multiply by a prime number to keep the hash distribution even. Then it takes every single entry from the old table and recomputes its index into the new table using the same hash function (now operating modulo the new, larger size). Each key gets a new slot, the load factor drops back down to roughly half its peak, and collisions are redistributed. The old table is discarded. For a well-behaved hash function the work of rehashing is roughly O(n) and the resize itself is rare — it only happens every time the table fills up, so amortized over many insertions it still works out to an average of O(1) per operation. The whole point of this resizing is to preserve that "most lookups are one step" property for as long as possible, and to kick in just before the collision-handling step would start to dominate the cost.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array of fixed size, but since the hash function is just a mathematical shortcut, two different keys can land in the same slot. That's a collision, and the map has to decide what to do when it finds one.

When a lookup or insertion hashes to an already-occupied slot, the map simply walks down that list comparing keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. When a collision occurs, the map probes outward—checking the next slot, or the next slot in a pattern defined by a secondary hash—until it finds an empty slot to use, or an existing slot with the same key to update. This avoids the extra allocation of separate lists and keeps everything in contiguous memory, which is cache-friendly. The downside is that clusters of occupied slots make subsequent probes slower, so implementations usually pair it with a good probing sequence and a load factor low enough to avoid that.

Most implementations set a threshold around 0.6 to 0.75. When an insertion pushes the load factor past that threshold, the map resizes: it allocates a new, larger array—usually double the previous size—and re-hashes every single existing entry into the new layout. Every key is re-inserted, so in a chaining implementation each entry is re-placed into its newly hashed bucket and re-appended to that bucket's list; in open addressing it simply lands in a fresh probe sequence. The old array is then discarded, and the next few insertions can proceed against the sparser table before the load factor is threatened again.

When a large language model generates text one token at a time, each step requires a full forward pass through the network before the next token can even be started. The model can't "guess ahead" because every future token depends on the last one being confirmed. On a GPU with thousands of cores sitting mostly idle during a single-token inference, that sequential bottleneck makes generation feel painfully slow.

Speculative decoding exploits the fact that in most text, the next token is highly predictable. The idea is to use a small, fast "draft" model to propose a whole short sequence of tokens in one go—say six of them—much faster than the large model could produce them one at a time. Then you feed that entire candidate sequence into the large model, which can evaluate all six tokens in a single parallel pass, since they're all already "written" and only need to be checked against the true context. The large model accepts or rejects each token in the proposal: if it agrees, those tokens are kept; if not, generation restarts at the first mismatch with the original next-token computation.

Nothing here changes what the large model would have produced. The large model is the sole decision-maker; the small model never writes any output that isn't explicitly vetted. It's essentially a parallelism trick disguised as a guess-and-check loop. In the common case where the draft gets several tokens right, you've effectively converted N sequential passes of the big model into one parallel pass plus a handful of small-model passes, and the final character stream is byte-for-byte identical to what you'd get from straightforward autoregressive sampling.

The key intuition for the new engineer: you're not replacing the big model with a cheap one. You're using the cheap one as a "fast forward" button so the expensive model can review a whole paragraph at once instead of one word at a time, while still holding the veto.

plain.content:
A hash map computes an integer hash for each key, maps that integer to a slot in a fixed-size array, and stores the value in (or near) that slot. The problem it must solve is that two entirely different keys can hash to the same slot, which is a collision. One common resolution is called chaining: every slot in the array holds the head of a small linked list (or similar container) of all the entries whose keys hashed to that position. To look something up, you compute the hash, jump to the slot, and then compare keys one by one down the list until you find a match or reach the end. The other major strategy is open addressing, in which the table is expected to hold only one entry per slot, and when your slot is already occupied you probe outward using a deterministic sequence (for example, check the next slot, then the one after that, or use a second hash function to jump around the array) until you land on an empty cell. Both approaches work, but they push the cost in different directions: chaining lets a single slot hold many entries without wasting space, while open addressing keeps the per-slot bookkeeping simple but demands that the table stay somewhat empty so probes don't drift far.

Resizing is the map's way of keeping those collisions and probes manageable over time. It watches a metric called the load factor, which is the number of entries divided by the number of slots in the underlying array. Once that ratio crosses a threshold chosen by the implementation (a value like 0.75 is very common), the map allocates a larger array—typically double the old one—recomputes the index for every single entry against the new, larger array, and swaps its reference to point at the new table. That rehashing pass means, for a moment, that every entry is touched, so the operation costs O(n) in the number of entries; but because it happens only when the table fills past the threshold and the next resizing doesn't occur until the table roughly doubles again in entry count, the amortized cost per insert, remove, or lookup stays at O(1). Some implementations also watch for the opposite problem: if entries are removed and the load factor falls well below the threshold, they may shrink the array down again to reclaim memory, taking care to use a lower "shrink" threshold than the "grow" one so the map doesn't oscillate between growing and shrinking on small additions and deletions.
